subject: Career
title: Sponsorship vs. Mentorship at Work
description: A 60-second lesson on Sponsorship vs. Mentorship at Work.

hook.text: A mentor gives advice. A sponsor gives opportunities. One talks to you. The other talks about you.

buildup.text: Sylvia Ann Hewlett's research shows sponsorship is the number one predictor of career advancement.

discovery.text: Sponsors advocate for you in rooms you're not in. They put their reputation behind your promotion.

twist.text: You can't ask for a sponsor directly. You earn sponsorship by delivering results that make them look good.

climax.text: Find a senior leader whose success depends on your work. Deliver excellence. Sponsorship follows.

punchline.text: Mentors guide your thinking. Sponsors change your trajectory.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between a mentor and a sponsor?
options: A sponsor advocates for you in rooms you're not in

details.summary: Mentors advise you behind closed doors, while sponsors publicly advocate for you in rooms you are not in. Research shows sponsorship is the more powerful career accelerator because it directly creates opportunities rather than just offering guidance.
details.whyItMatters: Many professionals invest in mentors but neglect to cultivate sponsors, missing the advocacy that drives promotions, stretch assignments, and leadership opportunities.
takeaways: Sponsors put their own reputation on the line to advocate for you
You earn sponsorship through consistently excellent visible work
Aim to have at least one sponsor two levels above your current position

faq.question: How do you find a sponsor rather than just a mentor in your organization?
faq.answer: Sponsors are earned, not asked for. Deliver exceptional visible work that leaders notice, volunteer for high-stakes projects they care about, and make their priorities your priorities. When a senior leader sees you as an extension of their success, sponsorship follows naturally.

faq.question: Can one person serve as both your mentor and your sponsor?
faq.answer: Yes, and this combination is especially powerful. However, the roles require different behaviors. A mentor listens and advises in private. A sponsor vocally champions you in meetings and decisions. Make sure your mentor-sponsor knows you value both forms of support.
